rationale: A wins because it keeps the facts on the page and does not decorate the update into a broader platform fantasy. Its best angle, "Discord undercuts Apple and Google, charging creators a 10% cut instead of 30%," is clean, timely, and properly bounded; B's "Undercuts App Stores and Patreon — But Can It Hold?" smuggles in Patreon, Twitch, YouTube, sustainability, and regulatory heat that the update did not supply. B has usable bones, but it keeps reaching for market narrative before it has evidence.
gaps_in_A: "Discord's new subscription tool doubles as a pre-IPO revenue pitch" is directionally fair, but it leans hard on "reportedly preparing for an IPO" without a sourced timeline; A does flag that proof need, which saves it from being reckless.

"Discord's move signals monetization is coming for the whole server, not just the streamer" is a bit thesis-y; the update supports community monetization, but "the whole server" needs examples before it becomes more than a smart frame.

A could use a sharper human/customer angle. The server-owner story is present, but framed around missing earnings data rather than the labor of community managers who might actually make the piece vivid.
gaps_in_B: "Patreon and Twitch" and later "YouTube" are invented comparison sets. The update only gives Apple/Google's 30% app-store standard, so B's competitive map is overstuffed.
"The company explicitly compares this to the 30% app-store standard" is not in the update. The facts say the fee is below the standard; they do not say Discord made that comparison.
"Millions of Unpaid Gaming Community Managers" is a big, shiny claim with no count, no source, and no proof that those managers are unpaid. That is headline-shaped hallucination.

"Discord Was Built for Gamers" and "Its Creator Subscription Launch Is a Bet It Can Be Patreon" rely on brand-history and competitor-positioning context not supplied in the update. It may be true in the world; it is not grounded here.
